column4: The section's dictionary image calls Suhā too faint to notice; the night sky's “النَّجْمُ الثَّاقِبُ” is instead a piercing star, a specific brightness reversal that makes the overlooked star's faintness salient.

The section says the Al-Alaq scene opens with its own “Have you seen”; this ayah opens that scene with “أَرَأَيْتَ,” echoing the source section's seeing question while turning sight toward a person who obstructs prayer.
The section says the Al-Alaq scene brings prayer into the meeting: this continuation identifies the obstructed one as “عَبْدًا إِذَا صَلَّىٰ,” making the blocked act explicit.
The section says the Al-Alaq scene adds a path interrupted midway; the next conditional asks whether the praying servant was “عَلَى الْهُدَىٰ,” giving that path a specific direction toward guidance.

The source's interrupted way also has an ethical destination: this continuation asks whether the servant “أَمَرَ بِالتَّقْوَىٰ,” so the obstruction reaches beyond the prayer act to a call to heed God.

The source section brings denial and turning away into its account of false religion; this ayah asks whether the obstructer “كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ,” joining denial to withdrawal in the same prayer-blocking scene.
The section sets public looking against the wish not to be overlooked; the scene closes, “بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ يَرَىٰ,” with God's sight as the boundary on human display.
The section explicitly links the orphan-pushing verb in 107:2 to fire: here the same root, د-ع-ع, is used as people are driven “إِلَىٰ نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ,” making the treatment rebound on its actors.
The section pairs denial with fire; this ayah calls it “هَٰذِهِ النَّارُ” that they had denied, making the denied consequence present before them.
The section connects the failure to urge food with a fire sentence; the account orders, “ثُمَّ الْجَحِيمَ صَلُّوهُ,” turning that same person's reckoning into punishment.
The source cites the same person's fire-account at 69:31; this continuation specifies that he is bound in a chain, carrying the punishment scene forward before the account names his neglected duties.
In the same reckoning invoked by the section, this ayah names the person's failure to believe in God before the next verse names the poor he did not feed; it joins denied faith to denied care.
The section directly links fire to failure to urge food; this ayah repeats “لَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ,” with the same ḥ-ḍ-ḍ root as its source wording, in that condemned man's account.
The section says the images return as one confession from inside the fire; this is the question that frames it: “مَا سَلَكَكُمْ فِي سَقَرَ,” asking the condemned what led them there.
The source's empty, outward prayer returns as a confession: “لَمْ نَكُ مِنَ الْمُصَلِّينَ.” The inmates themselves name the missing prayer among the causes of their being in Saqar.
The section's closed mouth around the poor's meal returns as “لَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ الْمِسْكِينَ”; their confession turns withheld feeding into an acknowledged cause of the fire.
The section's gloss “gaflete dalmak” meets this confession of “نَخُوضُ مَعَ الْخَائِضِينَ”: they went along with those who indulged, adding shared heedlessness to the private failures.
The section starts from denial of the reckoning; the inmates say “نُكَذِّبُ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ,” using the same k-dh-b root as 107:1 to state that denial from inside the fire.
The section presents the preceding answers as the account of how they reached the fire; their next words say this continued “حَتَّىٰ أَتَانَا الْيَقِينُ,” giving the confession its endpoint in death.
The section identifies the shelter verb for the orphan here: “فَآوَىٰ” says God found the addressee orphaned and gave him refuge, the protective act opposite the pushed-away child.

The section notes the same shelter verb for Mary and her son: “وَآوَيْنَاهُمَا” gives them refuge, while “قَرَارٍ وَمَعِينٍ” joins settled shelter to a flowing spring, meeting its home-and-water image.
The section shows a hand pushing the orphan away; “فَلَا تَقْهَرِ الْيَتِيمَ” reverses that act with a direct command not to oppress the orphan.
Beside the command about the orphan, “فَلَا تَنْهَرِ السَّائِلَ” forbids driving off a petitioner; it reverses the source section's refusal to open the way to a needy person.

The section pictures the orphan as pushed outside protection; this ayah says “إِصْلَاحٌ لَّهُمْ خَيْرٌ” and calls orphans brothers when they share a household, replacing expulsion with care and fellowship.
The section joins an orphan's treatment to fire; this verse makes that bond concrete in another way, saying those who unjustly consume orphans' property “إِنَّمَا يَأْكُلُونَ فِي بُطُونِهِمْ نَارًا.”
The section says the dim, vulnerable orphan is passed over; this rebuke states “لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ,” naming failure to honor the orphan as the very social fault at issue.
Where the source says the person does not urge food for the poor, this ayah says “وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ,” repeating the h-ḍ-ḍ root as a communal failure to encourage feeding.

The section pairs neglect of the orphan with withholding small aid; the next charge in this same rebuke is consuming inheritance “أَكْلًا لَّمًّا,” extending the scene to taking what should be protected.

The section links overlooked people with a hand that withholds; this continuation says the people “تُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا,” naming attachment to wealth alongside the neglected orphan and poor.
The section's withheld household help meets a passage about those who are stingy and conceal God's bounty; “يَبْخَلُونَ” and “يَكْتُمُونَ” give withholding a material and hidden side.

The section makes a show-prayer image central; this neighboring description says people spend “رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ,” using the same r-ʾ-y root as the source's display word and applying it to visible giving.
This ayah joins the section's distracted prayer and its “for show” image in one description: hypocrites come to prayer lazily, “يُرَاءُونَ النَّاسَ,” and remember God only a little.
The source links display to a path cut short; this warning names those who leave home in arrogance and “رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ” while barring others from God's way, joining public display to obstruction.

The section contrasts attention-seeking prayer with neglected need; this ayah shows ostentatious charity “رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ” that leaves no lasting benefit when rain strips a rock bare, so being seen does not itself feed anyone.

The section's prayer is done for human eyes, but this ayah draws a specific boundary: open charity is good, while concealing it and giving it to the poor is better, distinguishing visibility from its purpose and recipient.
The Al-Alaq scene in the section is about obstructing a praying servant; this ayah broadens that boundary to those who prevent God's name from being remembered in mosques and work for their ruin.

The section separates empty prayer from withheld aid; this account of hypocrites puts the failures together: they approach prayer lazily and spend only reluctantly, linking ritual neglect with a closed hand.
The section develops “سَاهُونَ” (root s-h-w) as heedlessness in the field of seeing; this verse uses the same form for people in heedlessness, and its following question is about the Day of Judgment.

The section joins prayer-neglect to denial of reckoning; continuing the “heedless” description, this verse asks “أَيَّانَ يَوْمُ الدِّينِ,” putting their heedlessness beside the very day they dispute.
Against the section's prayer performed for onlookers, the God-fearing in this passage sleep little at night; this quiet, unseen discipline is a specific opposite to worship staged for people.
The same night-devotion passage says they ask forgiveness before dawn; this private turning toward God contrasts with the section's prayer whose heart is absent and audience is human.

The section understands small aid as a due in wealth; this verse says the God-fearing have “حَقٌّ مَّعْلُومٌ” in their property for the asker and deprived, joining inner devotion to a specified right for others.
The section's withholding root appears in this portrait: when good reaches a person, he is “مَنُوعًا,” showing the same m-n-ʿ restraint that culminates in withholding al-ma'un.
The section sets hollow prayer against a real devotional circle; after describing the withholding person, this passage exempts “الْمُصَلِّينَ,” the worshippers who answer that tendency.
The section's false prayer is bounded by people who remain constant in prayer: “عَلَىٰ صَلَاتِهِمْ دَائِمُونَ” describes continuing worship rather than prayer that is neglected.
The section glosses al-ma'un as a due; this ayah says such people have “حَقٌّ مَّعْلُومٌ” in their wealth, making giving a recognized right rather than optional display.
The preceding known right is for “السَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ”; this continuation identifies the very claimant and deprived person whom the section's withheld help leaves unseen.
The section begins with people denying the Day of Recompense; the same devotional profile says they “يُصَدِّقُونَ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ,” making belief in that day part of the repaired circle.

The section says the share, prayer, and reassurance form a broken circle; here the Messenger is told to take charity and pray for its givers, and “إِنَّ صَلَاتَكَ سَكَنٌ لَّهُمْ” names that prayer as their comfort.

The section's disconnected prayer, orphan, poor, and denial are gathered here into *birr*: giving to kin, orphans, and poor, establishing prayer, giving zakah, and believing in the Last Day belong to one truthful pattern.
The section shows a meal withheld from the poor; this passage reverses the act by feeding the needy, orphan, and captive, making practical care the visible counterpart to withholding.
The section's worshippers seek human notice; these givers say they feed only for God's face and seek neither reward nor thanks, clarifying the intention that the source's show-prayer lacks.
The same givers say they fear a frowning, difficult day from their Lord; this continues the reversal of those who deny the reckoning at the heart of the section.
Where the section says no one urges food for the poor, this passage makes feeding during famine a passage through hardship, reversing neglect with a concrete act of provision.
The next detail specifies that the hungry one is an orphan “ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ,” closely joining food to care for the vulnerable child in the section.
The continuing list names a needy person “ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ”; it makes visible the socially lowly person whom the section says is overlooked.
The section's person does not encourage feeding; this passage praises believers who “تَوَاصَوْا بِالْمَرْحَمَةِ,” urging one another to mercy and forming a supportive circle.

The section says hypocritical-looking people withhold the small aid; this description of hypocrite men and women says they forbid right and “يَقْبِضُونَ أَيْدِيَهُمْ,” explicitly joining obstruction to hands held closed.

Against the closed hands and obstruction of the preceding hypocrites, believing men and women help one another, establish prayer, and give zakah; the verse states the mutual circle the section says has broken.

The section's men pray for human eyes; here trade does not distract the believers from God's remembrance, prayer, and zakah, and they fear a Day when hearts and eyes turn over, a specific inward-facing counter-image.
The section's prayer is empty and performed for an audience; this passage marks the successful believers by humility “فِي صَلَاتِهِمْ خَاشِعُونَ,” a direct reversal in the prayer itself.
The same profile continues by giving zakah, turning the section's withheld al-ma'un into an active duty within a sound prayerful life.
The profile ends this list by guarding its prayers; that care reverses the section's people who let prayer slip from their attention.
The section contrasts prayer for people's eyes with prayer's inward purpose; God commands prayer “لِذِكْرِي,” for His remembrance, giving the act a different addressee and aim.
The section's show-prayer is bounded by the command to worship God with sincere devotion, establish prayer, and give zakah; this verse joins the same acts under “مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ الدِّينَ.”
The section reads al-ma'un as a small obligation; this warning concerns people who short the measure, a concrete case of withholding what another is due.
The section says the person denies another's small right yet seeks not to be overlooked; this ayah specifies the asymmetry: he takes full measure when receiving from others.
Continuing that asymmetry, the trader gives others less in the scale; the section's withheld aid and performed self-importance meet here as giving less while expecting full treatment.
The section links denied dues with denial of a reckoning; the measure-fraud passage next asks whether these people think they will be raised, making the ethical accounting answerable to a final one.
The same question specifies “لِيَوْمٍ عَظِيمٍ”; this continues the reckoning frame that the section joins to the withheld small right.
The passage concludes that all people stand before the Lord of the worlds; that scene gives the section's contrast between being seen by people and answerable to God a concrete endpoint.
The section's ma'un includes a due in wealth and small assistance; this warning addresses those who hoard gold and silver instead of spending in God's way, extending withheld help to hoarded wealth.
The hoarding passage continues with the treasure heated in Hell and used to brand its owners; it completes the section's meeting of withheld wealth and fire with a concrete judgment scene.

The section's lexicographic reading of ma'un includes a small thing lent or owed; this verse calls giving wealth for God's cause “قَرْضًا حَسَنًا,” a distinct, metaphorical loan that extends the image from neighborly aid to accountable giving.

The section's dictionary sense of ma'un includes a small loan; this repeated Quranic image asks who will give God “قَرْضًا حَسَنًا,” extending the domestic lending image to wealth entrusted for God's reward.
The section's dictionary sense of ma'un includes a small loan; this verse likewise says “تُقْرِضُوا اللَّهَ قَرْضًا حَسَنًا,” carrying that lending image into giving that God multiplies and forgives.
The section's dictionary sense of ma'un includes a small loan; this verse asks for a good loan to God, placing material giving within the obedient service that the section joins to al-ma'un.

The section joins being overlooked with wanting to be seen; this ayah opens a scene with a person turning away, and the continuation reveals that his attention had gone to the self-sufficient while a vulnerable visitor waited.
This continuation identifies the arriving person as blind; the section's missed orphan and poor similarly stand at the edge of another's attention, though this ayah's visitor is not said to be poor.
The section says the person looked past can contain an unseen inner life; this continuation asks whether the blind visitor might become purified, making his potential a reason not to dismiss him.
The same visitor might remember and benefit from a reminder; this adds the possible spiritual benefit that the neglecting gaze in the section fails to see.

The section's vulnerable people are passed over while its actors seek notice; the next figure in this scene is one who considers himself self-sufficient, the socially powerful person whose attention draws the gaze.
This ayah says attention is directed toward that self-sufficient figure; it identifies where the gaze went in the scene of overlooking the blind visitor.

The passage bounds the preacher's responsibility by saying he is not accountable if the self-sufficient man refuses purification; that distinction helps keep the section's failure of care separate from the recipient's response.
The passage turns to another arrival, one who comes striving; this keeps the focus on the person who actively seeks attention after the well-positioned figure received it.
This arriving person fears God; the detail makes his inward seriousness visible in the very scene where the gaze is diverted from him.
The ayah says attention is diverted from the striving, God-fearing arrival; this is the same specific failure of sight and attention developed by the section's overlooked vulnerable people.

The section says needy people are overlooked as faint; this verse describes poor people whose restraint makes the uninformed think they are self-sufficient, though they can be recognized by their signs and do not persistently ask.
The section depicts a hand driving the vulnerable away; this command forbids driving away people who call on their Lord morning and evening, protecting their place in the gathering.

This command says to stay with those who call on their Lord and not let one's eyes pass beyond them for worldly adornment; it meets the section's eyes-for-people image with a direct boundary on whom to keep in view.
The section says an orphan has lost a protective circle; this verse makes the guardian's concrete duty to deliver orphans' property and not consume it part of that protection.
Continuing the orphan-care rules, this ayah requires testing until maturity and handing over property when judgment is sound; it specifies how a guardian preserves what belongs to the child.
Alongside its command for just measure, this ayah forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best way until maturity, joining protection of the vulnerable to a measured due.

This repeated command likewise forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best way until maturity; it makes the lost-guardian image concrete as a continuing duty to safeguard the child's resources.

The section's shelter image meets the story of a wall built for two orphans so their treasure remains protected until they mature; the verse makes hidden, future provision a reason to preserve a place for children.
The section reads al-ma'un as zakah and a due; this verse assigns zakah among the poor, needy, debtors, and other named recipients, specifying how a share reaches people who need it.
The section's dictionary gloss includes a tight-handed person; this command pictures the hand chained to the neck and forbids that restraint, setting generosity between withholding and waste.

The section says its actors want not to be overlooked while denying the Day; after such people forget their meeting with that Day, this verse says they will be forgotten and their refuge is the Fire, a direct reversal of their wish to remain seen.
The section shows people withholding small help; this verse tells people of means not to swear off giving to relatives, the needy, and migrants, and urges pardon, directly reversing the closed hand.

The section gathers care for vulnerable people, prayer, and zakah into a broken circle; this covenant joins worship, care for orphans and poor people, good speech, prayer, and zakah, then notes that most turned away.
This command joins worship of God with goodness to orphans and needy people, then condemns arrogant self-display; it gathers the section's social duties and outward-looking failure in one address.

The chiefs reject Noah's followers as the lowest people and say they see no distinction in them; this scene explicitly stages the social gaze that discounts the lowly whom the section says are passed over.
Noah answers that he will not drive away the believers; the verse directly reverses the section's pushing away of the vulnerable and says those believers will meet their Lord.
Noah asks who would protect him from God if he drove the believers away; this continuation ties refusal to expel the lowly to the protection image developed around the orphan.
Noah refuses to declare that those whom people's eyes scorn will receive no good from God; this directly challenges the section's way of overlooking the dim and vulnerable.
